added_claim_errors: Applies the 3.6% January 2027 COLA to her $2,400 estimate as certain ($2,486, then $1,740/month). The key flags this as a trap; the right figure is about $1,690.
Says 70% from '60 months gives exactly 168/240'. She starts April 2027, which is 59 months early (29.58%). Acceptable as an approximation, but stated as exact.

Table shows $1,222 of Social Security in every month of 2027, with $518/month withholding spread over 12 months. No benefits are paid January to March and SSA withholds whole checks, and the table contradicts the answer's own $7,700 annual figure.
'Roughly three and a half of them get swallowed': SSA withholds whole checks, so it is four checks, with the small excess repaid later.
'You'll lose that $6,220 every year until March 2032': the limit rises every year, the FRA year uses a higher limit and a $1-for-$3 rule, and withheld benefits are not simply lost.
'Waiting to 67 would pay $2,486': this ignores COLAs between now and 2032. Minor.
Federal tax estimate assumes $14,664 of benefits received in 2027, but actual 2027 receipts are lower. Labelled as an estimate; minor.
Applies the 3.6% January 2027 COLA to her $2,400 estimate as certain ($2,486, then $1,740/month). The key flags this as a trap; the right figure is about $1,690.
Says claiming at 62 pays 70%. She is 59 months early (29.58%). Acceptable approximation.
Table shows $1,222 of Social Security in every month of 2027 with smoothed $518/month withholding, though no benefits come January to March and whole checks are withheld.
'About $1,740/month less before tax, roughly $1,500 less after' is arithmetic error. $5,567 - $4,389 = $1,178 before tax; $5,567 - $3,824 = $1,743 after tax.

'Calendar 2027 will deliver about $9,400' counts nine months (April to December) less $6,220. The December benefit is paid in January 2028 and the excess is refunded later, so 2027 cash receipts are about $6,960.
'Drop to about $25,500 ... come out roughly even on cash' is wrong. Giving up about $12,500 in wages to keep $6,220 in benefits is a net loss of about $6,280 before tax.
'Budget $500-900/month' for health insurance is unverifiable and unsourced; it depends heavily on location and subsidies.
'You'll lose that $6,220 every year until March 2032': the limit is indexed each year and the FRA-year rules differ.
'Waiting to 67 pays about $2,486' ignores COLAs to 2032. Minor.

reasons: The two answers are nearly identical. Both correct both premises at the start, give the right 2027 earnings-test figures ($25,560 limit, $12,440 excess, $6,220 withheld) and the April 2027 start, and both fall into the COLA trap ($1,740 instead of about $1,690). Both also show a smoothed table that hides the first months with no Social Security, and neither points her to SSA's calculators or her my Social Security account. B adds substantive errors that A avoids: the shortfall comparison is miscomputed ('$1,740 less before tax' when it is $1,178), it says cutting hours would leave her 'roughly even' when that is a net loss of about $6,280, and it gives an unsourced $500-900 health-insurance range. A gets the hours trade-off and the before-tax gap right and cites its tax brackets. B's 'four checks' matches the key slightly better than A's 'three and a half', but that does not outweigh B's arithmetic and advice errors.
